newsitem.title: UK: UK's rich play safe ahead of expected Labour win.
newsitem.headline: UK's rich play safe ahead of expected Labour win.

text.p: Britain's rich are accelerating tax planning ahead of an expected Labour election victory but consultants say few are taking the drastic action they would once have contemplated under "Old Labour".

Labour under Tony Blair has started to dismantle its tax-and-spend image and court the wealthy -- a sharp contrast to promises by Labour Chancellor of the Exchequer Denis Healey in the 1970s to "squeeze the rich until the pips squeak".

"A number of clients two years ago were talking about the possibility of emigrating if we had a Labour government. I don't think any of them will seriously do that," said Elspeth May, personal financial services partner at KPMG, told Reuters.
But Labour's pledge not to increase income tax rates for five years has raised concerns about other measures, which consultants say are likely to come in the form of capital tax changes.

Wealthy clients are being advised to get their affairs in order ahead of the new financial year, as the current tax regime was likely to be the most favourable for some time. Prime Minister John Major must call a general election by May 22.
May said many clients had stepped up their tax planning with Labour's main focus expected to be on capital taxes, but were not overly concerned about a change of government.

"They have either been persuaded that things aren't going to be that bad or there isn't that much more that they can do," said May, who mostly manages clients worth between one to ten million sterling.
Other players say there is very little UK residents, with assets totalling tens of billion of pounds, can now legally do to avoid fresh taxation measures.
"UK clients are rabbits in the headlights," Jonathan Colchester, marketing director at Credit Suisse Private Banking told Reuters.

Benchmarking firm Compare says that at the end of 1995, some 70 billion sterling was tied up in personal accounts worth over 250,000 sterling at brokers registered with the LSE. Of that, 48.5 billion is in over 25,000 accounts holding more than 600,000 sterling.
Allowing for growth in line with the rise in the FTSE since then, the 70 billion is probably now worth over 100 billion.

Analysts expect a major focus of Labour to be moves to get non-domiciled UK residents into the tax net. Currently, only UK earnings are subject to tax and capital gains and inheritance taxes can be avoided if housed offshore.
"Labour have specifically said that they are going tighten loopholes and screw down people who are living here without paying tax," UBS vice-president Richard Madeley said.
"I tend to think that to do so would be a massive own goal and they might find that when they get there and actually try and do it they'll be lobbied very, very hard."

Colchester said the effect of a major tightening on non-domiciles could be to simply drive them out of the country, which would serve little purpose as the sector helped fuel the UK retail and service markets.
Analysts cite Britain's bloodstock industry as one that would suffer on attempts to tighten up on non-domiciles.
"Half of that industry in the UK is found on non-domicile capital," a tax consultant said.
An area that Labour is expected to clamp down on is on UK residents leaving the country, currently for between one and three years, to avoid tax on realised capital gains in the period.
"The Labour party have said they are going to clamp straight down on it and that can easily be backdated. If you are not non-resident this year it is too late," UBS's Madeley said.
Portfolio shifts by the rich are similar to those at major institutions, fund managers say, with moves out of sectors that are unlikely to get Labour support.

These include restructuring stocks, said Credit Suisse's Colchester. He said the major beneficiary of these companies' efforts to restructure, and often shed jobs, are shareholders, which have "never been Labour's constituency."
"Much more client money is in growth companies where they think they are going to get better returns."
Other players say utilities, targeted for windfall taxes by Labour, are also being shed.

Price Waterhouse personal tax head John Whiting said an area facing a clampdown is reinvestment relief, where tax on the realisation of a gain can be avoided by reinvesting in an unquoted company to avoid capital gains tax.
He said there could be restrictions placed on the sort of companies, the amount to be rolled into the investment, or a time limit on how long the rollover could last.
Whiting said capital gains tax changes were likely to take effect from the date of announcement.

"The worst case scenario is that Gordon Brown stands up on June 6 for his mini-budget and says I am cancelling reinvestment relief. It is 99.9 percent certain anything you have done up to that point is okay. If you are considering reinvestment relief then make sure you accelerate it." -- London newsroom +171 542 5887
